**Options on the formatter overview page**
- `line-length`: maximum line width; the formatter wraps code to fit it.
- `quote-style`: preferred string quote character, for example `"single"`.
- `indent-style`: spaces or tabs for indentation.
- `docstring-code-format`: formats Python code examples inside docstrings.
- `docstring-code-line-length`: line limit for those docstring examples, or `"dynamic"` to follow `line-length`.
- `nested-string-quote-style`: quoting for nested strings in f-string expressions; applies on Python 3.12+.
- `preview` (shown as `format_preview` in the overview): opts into the unstable preview style.
- `extension`: maps custom file extensions, such as `mdx` or `qmd`, to Markdown formatting. This is a general setting, not formatter-specific.
- `extend-exclude`: skips files, such as `*.md`, during formatting. This is also a general setting.

**Extra options in the settings reference**
- `format.line-ending`: line-ending style: `auto`, `lf`, `crlf` or `native` (default `auto`).
- `format.skip-magic-trailing-comma`: ignores existing trailing commas when deciding whether to keep a collection split across lines (default `false`).
- `format.exclude`: file patterns to skip when formatting, on top of the global excludes (default `[]`).

**Vercel gives more bandwidth on the free tier: 100 GB per month, against roughly 15 GB on Netlify.**

- **Vercel (Hobby plan):** It includes 100 GB per month of Fast Data Transfer, which is data delivered to end users. There are separate allowances on top of that: 10 GB of Fast Origin Transfer and 10 GB of Blob Data Transfer.
- **Netlify (Free plan):** It uses a shared credit system, with a 300-credit limit and no stated bandwidth figure. Bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB, so 300 credits works out to about 15 GB. That figure only holds if bandwidth is the only thing you use. Deploys (15 credits each), compute and requests draw from the same 300 credits.

The Netlify number is my calculation from the credit rates on the page, not a figure Netlify states. The page also didn't say whether the credits reset monthly. Vercel's Hobby plan also can't buy extra usage, so you'd have to upgrade if you hit its cap.

The newest version I found is **Tailwind CSS v4.3.1**, released June 12, 2026. That comes from a single search, and it's now October 2026, so a newer patch may exist. You can confirm on the npm `tailwindcss` package or the GitHub releases page.

The big change was **v4.0** (January 2025), the last major version. These are the main points, and I'm giving them from my own knowledge, not from the search:

- **New engine:** It was rewritten (called "Oxide", with parts in Rust) and is much faster. Full builds are several times faster, and incremental builds are orders of magnitude faster.
- **CSS-first configuration:** You configure it in your CSS with `@theme` and `@import "tailwindcss"` instead of a `tailwind.config.js`. Design tokens are exposed as native CSS variables.
- **Simpler setup:** Content detection is automatic, so you don't list template paths. There's also a first-party Vite plugin, and you no longer need separate PostCSS plugins like autoprefixer or `postcss-import`.
- **Modern CSS features:** It builds on cascade layers, `@property`, and `color-mix()`. It also adds container queries, 3D transforms, and expanded gradient utilities.
- **Breaking changes:** It drops support for older browsers, and some utilities were renamed or removed. An upgrade tool is available.

The 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 releases have been incremental on top of that.

**Best starting points**
1. **[Research and analysis of performance of LLM on the Raspberry Pi 5](https://stratospherelinuxips.readthedocs.io/en/develop/immune/research_rpi_llm_performance.html)** (Stratosphere lab). This is the most rigorous write-up I found. It says Ollama's defaults (such as a 4096-token context) aren't tuned for low-resource devices. It cites llama.cpp as roughly 10–20% faster than Ollama, and the project chose llama.cpp for that reason.
2. **[Run Llama3-8b on a Raspberry Pi 5 with ExecuTorch](https://dev-discuss.pytorch.org/t/run-llama3-8b-on-a-raspberry-pi-5-with-executorch/2048)** (PyTorch forum). It reports about 2 tokens/sec for a 4-bit Llama 3 8B. Arm has a step-by-step tutorial for the same approach: [Arm learning path](https://learn.arm.com/learning-paths/embedded-and-microcontrollers/rpi-llama3/run/).
3. **[Run LLMs on Raspberry Pi 5](https://tinyweights.dev/posts/run-llms-raspberry-pi-5/)** (tinyweights.dev). It's a practical llama.cpp guide that estimates 5–15 tokens/sec for 1.5B models and 2–5 for 3B models. It explains that generation speed is limited by memory bandwidth. I couldn't check those numbers against another source.

**Also useful**
- **[TinyLlama and Llama3 with Raspberry Pi 5](https://learn.littlebirdelectronics.com.au/guides/tinyllama-with-raspberry-pi-5)** is a beginner-friendly Ollama walkthrough. It notes Llama 3 is much slower than TinyLlama on the Pi.
- **[Ollama vs llama.cpp on Raspberry Pi 5](https://medium.com/@omkar121212/ollama-vs-llama-cpp-on-raspberry-pi-5-8e7fbeb310de)** is a Medium comparison that found llama.cpp faster than Ollama on TinyLlama 1.1B.
- **[SitePoint: LLMs on Raspberry Pi edge](https://www.sitepoint.com/llms-raspberry-pi-edge/)** covers running llama-server as an OpenAI-compatible API.
- **[arXiv 2511.07425](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.07425v1)** benchmarks 25 quantized models on Pi 4, Pi 5 and Orange Pi 5 Pro. It concludes these boards handle models up to about 1.5B parameters reliably. It also found Llamafile gave up to 4x the throughput of Ollama.

**Takeaways**
- Llama 3.2 1B and 3B are the sweet spot. One benchmark with Ollama reported about 11 tokens/sec for 1B and 4.7 for 3B (Q4_K_M).
- 8B models run, but at only about 2 tokens/sec.
- llama.cpp is generally faster than Ollama on the Pi.

8. **Strict Mode**: Strict mode turns off type coercion, so `'123'` is rejected for an `int` field. You can enable it per call, per field, or for a whole model, with field-level overrides.
9. **Unions**: Pydantic validates unions in three ways: left-to-right, smart mode (the default, which picks the best match), and discriminated unions. Discriminated unions are recommended for performance and predictability. The page also covers customizing union error messages.

   - This review isn't specific to fasting. It covers why weight loss in general costs lean mass (roughly 25% of the loss in typical diets), and what limits that loss: adequate protein and resistance exercise.

This is the "Attention Is All You Need" paper. In plain words, the abstract says:

- **The problem:** The best models for tasks like machine translation used complicated recurrent or convolutional neural networks. These had an encoder and a decoder, and often an attention mechanism linking the two.
- **The idea:** The authors propose a simpler architecture called the **Transformer**. It uses only attention mechanisms and drops recurrence and convolutions entirely.
- **The results:** On translation tasks, the Transformer produced better quality than existing models. That includes a new state-of-the-art score on English-to-French and strong results on English-to-German.
- **The efficiency:** Because it doesn't process words one at a time, it can be parallelized much more. That makes it far faster and cheaper to train.
- **Generality:** It also works well on a different task, English constituency parsing, which suggests it isn't limited to translation.

Here are three papers. I'm citing them from memory and haven't checked them against a database, so confirm the details (especially the numbers) before you rely on them.

1. **Lowe DA et al. (2020), *JAMA Internal Medicine*.** "Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial."
   - In this trial, 16:8 time-restricted eating produced no more weight loss than regular meal timing.
   - It also showed a loss of lean mass, including appendicular lean mass. This is the main paper behind the worry that IF can cost muscle.
   - Caveat: the trial was unsupervised and had no resistance training, and the lean mass measure was DXA.

2. **Moro T et al. (2016), *Journal of Translational Medicine*.** "Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males."
   - Fat mass fell, while fat-free mass and strength were maintained.
   - Caveat: the sample was small (34 men), and the men were already resistance-trained and kept lifting.

3. **Tinsley GM et al. (2017), *European Journal of Sport Science*.** "Time-restricted feeding in young men performing resistance training: A randomized controlled trial."
   - Time-restricted feeding was compared with normal eating while the men trained. Lean mass and strength didn't differ meaningfully between groups.
   - Caveat: the study was short and small.

**What they suggest together:** IF isn't clearly worse than ordinary calorie restriction for muscle. Losing weight by any method tends to cost some lean mass. The risk looks highest when protein intake is low and there's no resistance training, as in Lowe. Lifting and adequate protein seem to preserve muscle in the Moro and Tinsley studies.

- **Netlify (Free plan):** a pool of 300 credits, with no separate bandwidth cap. Bandwidth costs 20 credits per GB, so spending everything on bandwidth gets you about 15 GB. That figure is my calculation from the credit rate, not a number Netlify states.

**Bug fixes**
- Optional dependencies now export correctly when transitive extras are activated through different or incompatible environment paths (#22751).
- Invalid custom build cache keys now produce an error. Before, uv silently fell back to the defaults (#22749).

**The big change was v4.0, the last major release (January 2025).** Everything since is a minor or patch update on top of it. The main changes in v4.0:
- **New engine:** It is rewritten for performance, with much faster full builds and far faster incremental builds. This is the "Oxide" engine, which is partly written in Rust.
- **CSS-first configuration:** You configure the theme in your CSS with `@theme` instead of a `tailwind.config.js`. Setup is now just `@import "tailwindcss";` instead of the three `@tailwind` directives.
- **Simpler tooling:** There is a first-party Vite plugin, automatic content detection and no need for PostCSS plugins like autoprefixer.
- **Modern CSS underneath:** It uses native cascade layers, `@property` and `color-mix()`. Theme values are exposed as CSS variables.

**Takeaways**
- Speed is limited by memory bandwidth, since the Pi 5 has no GPU or NPU for inference.
- 1–3B Llama models are usable.
- 8B runs but is slow, at about 2 tok/s.

eld names for validation and serialization. They can be set with `alias`, `validation_alias`, `serialization_alias` or a model-wide `alias_generator`. Config and runtime flags decide whether aliases, field names or both are accepted and emitted.
- **Serialization**: `model_dump()` produces dicts and `model_dump_json()` produces JSON strings. You can customize output with field or model serializers. Include/exclude settings control which fields appear, including exclusion by value or by whether a field was explicitly set.
- **JSON**: Built-in JSON parsing uses the `jiter` parser through `model_validate_json` and `TypeAdapter.validate_json`. It also offers partial JSON parsing with `allow_partial=True` and configurable string caching.
- **JSON Schema**: Pydantic generates JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12 and OpenAPI 3.1) from models and types, in validation or serialization mode. You can customize it with `json_schema_extra`, `WithJsonSchema`, `SkipJsonSchema` or a `GenerateJsonSchema` subclass. The page also maps Python types to their schema equivalents.
- **Dataclasses**: `@pydantic.dataclasses.dataclass` adds validation to standard dataclasses and supports config, `Field()`, validators and inheritance. They lack `BaseModel` methods (use `TypeAdapter` instead), don't serialize extra data, and handle parameterized generics poorly.
- **Strict Mode**: Strict mode rejects data that isn't already the right type instead of coercing it, for example `'123'` for an `int`. You can enable it per call, per field or in model config, and fields can override the model-level setting.
- **Conversion Table**: This is a reference table of how input values are coerced into each type, in lax and strict modes, for both Python and JSON input. Each entry notes whether strict mode allows the conversion and any conditions.
- **Experimental Features**: This page covers a type-safe pipeline API for composing validation and transforms, and `generate_arguments_schema()` for validating a callable's arguments without calling it. It also covers partial validation for incomplete data such as streamed LLM output, which is still a proof of concept.
- **Forward Annotations**: This page covers referencing types defined later, or self-referencing models. Python 3.14+ resolves these lazily. Earlier versions need quoted names or `from __future__ import annotations`, plus `TYPE_CHECKING` blocks and `model_rebuild()` for cyclic cases.
- **Performance tips**: Suggestions include `model_validate_json()`, reusing `TypeAdapter` instances, preferring concrete types like `list` over abstract ones, and using tagged unions. It also advises avoiding wrap validators and unnecessary nesting, and using `FailFast`.
- **Settings Management**: Pydantic Settings defines typed config classes that load from environment variables, `.env` files, secrets directories and cloud secret stores. It also covers nested models, source priority and building CLIs from settings models. My fetch only read the first 100,000 of about 126,600 characters, so the last part of this page isn't reflected.
- **Type Adapter**: `TypeAdapter` validates, serializes and generates JSON schemas for non-`BaseModel` types like `list[Model]`, `TypedDict` or primitives. Create it once and reuse it, since building the schema is costly.
- **Unions**: Unions validate in one of three modes: left-to-right, smart (the default, which picks the best match), or discriminated. Discriminated unions are recommended for speed and predictability. `Discriminator` and `Tag` customize them and their errors.
- **Validation Decorator**: `validate_call()` checks and coerces a function's arguments against its annotations before the call. It supports all parameter kinds, async functions, `Field()` constraints and optional return validation. The original function stays reachable via `raw_function`, and the decorator adds some call overhead.
- **Validators** and **Models** are the core pages. **Types**, **Fields** and **Configuration** build on them.

Here are three papers I'm confident exist. I'm citing them from memory and haven't looked them up, so check the details before you rely on them.

1. **Lowe DA et al. (2020), *JAMA Network Open*: "Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial."**
   - This was a 12-week RCT of 16:8 eating compared with regular meals.
   - Time-restricted eating produced no significant extra weight loss. Lean mass fell in both groups, and appendicular lean mass fell more in the fasting group.
   - Many people cite it as a warning about lean-mass loss. The trial didn't include resistance training.

2. **Moro T et al. (2016), *Journal of Translational Medicine*: "Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males."**
   - This was a small study of resistance-trained men.
   - Fat mass dropped and fat-free mass and strength were maintained, which suggests that training can protect muscle.
   - The sample was small and the follow-up short, so treat it as preliminary.

3. **Cava E, Yeat NC, Mittendorfer B (2017), *Advances in Nutrition*: "Preserving Healthy Muscle during Weight Loss."**
   - This review covers why weight loss, however achieved, usually costs some lean mass (roughly a quarter of the weight lost in many studies).
   - It shows that protein intake and resistance exercise matter more for protecting muscle than the eating schedule does.

**Overall:** Intermittent fasting seems to cause about the same muscle loss as ordinary calorie restriction when calories are matched. Resistance training and adequate protein are what protect muscle. Most trials are short and small, and many measure lean mass with DXA, which counts water and other non-muscle tissue as lean mass.
